The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne. Leonardo's painting of the Virgin and Child with Saint Anne, completed around 1503 to 1519, depicts three generations—the grandmother Saint Anne, her daughter the Virgin Mary, and the infant Christ—unified in a pyramidal composition of extraordinary psychological complexity. The work represents Leonardo's mature synthesis of geometric harmony, sfumato technique, and tender human interaction within a sacred framework.

The painting is oil on poplar panel, measuring about 66 by 51 inches, and now hangs in the Louvre Museum in Paris. The composition is complex and three-figured, arranged pyramidally, with Saint Anne at the apex, Mary in the middle, and Christ and the lamb at the base. The landscape background is rendered in atmospheric perspective, receding into misty mountains and winding paths, creating a dreamlike spatial depth.

Christ playfully grasps the lamb, symbolizing his future sacrifice, while Mary gently restrains him, and Anne benignly observes, capturing both innocence and foreknowledge. Leonardo employed sfumato to create seamless transitions between figures and landscape, with soft modeling of flesh tones and a pervasive golden light. The work may have remained unfinished in Leonardo's eyes; he continually revised and perfected it, carrying it with him in his travels across Italy and France. The composition influenced countless later renderings of the subject and established Leonardo's mature approach to multi-figure sacred narrative.
